job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Carlos Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy, honestly. I wake up, check which of my 40 applications got a reply, then spend the morning on a freelance job: I build spreadsheet dashboards for small shops, using AI to write most of the formulas. Afternoons I play five-a-side with friends near the port, and in the evening I help my grandmother Abuela Rosa with her pension forms. I live in Port Selby with my parents and her.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you study, and what did you do on your internship?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Business and finance, with a good result. Last summer I did six weeks in the finance team of a freight company, cleaning up shipment costs. My final project was a sales dashboard for a food-truck co-op, and I used AI tools every day for it, which my professor allowed as long as I explained what each tool did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the hype was too big, but don't relax. At friends' tables I'd say the useful bits still matter, like faster reports and cleaner data, so learn them anyway. Online I'd post my dashboards and a couple of tips, because that's how I get freelance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my life carries on as it is: apply, freelance, wait. The routine parts of junior finance do get cheaper, though, so I want to be the person who sets up the routine work, not the person who does it by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the freelancing, pitch to six more shops this month, and aim the applications at firms that care about reporting and analysis. I'd also charge properly: I've been underpricing my work for months. And I'd keep helping Abuela Rosa because her forms take hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy, to be fair. I'm not anxious, just impatient to get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a shop pay you more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make a shop pay you more?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the freelancing feel like a career or a stopgap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A story with numbers. I fixed the stock sheet for a bakery and showed the owner she was losing about 200 a month on waste. She paid me for three more projects. If I can show that in a job interview, I won't need to beg.

say: I'd say the hype was too big but the useful bits, like faster **reports**, still matter.
I'd post my dashboards online to win freelance work.
think: My life carries on: apply, freelance, wait, but I want to **set up** routine tasks, not do them by hand.
I've been underpricing my work for months.
do: Pitch to **six more shops** this month and charge proper rates.
Aim applications at firms that value **reporting** and analysis.
Keep helping Abuela Rosa with her pension forms.

fieldNote: Treats AI as a **tool** he already controls, so the plateau barely touches him.

Impatience, not fear, is his main emotion.

steps.text: Pitch to six more small shops for dashboard work
Raise my freelance rate for the bakery and shop jobs
Apply to firms that value reporting and analysis
Learn the newest spreadsheet automation features

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: it takes the drudge work and leaves the judgment. I'd tell friends who are still applying to build something real, not just send CVs. At the same time, I'd say out loud that the gains should be shared, not locked in a few firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think many entry jobs shrink, including the ones I'm applying for. Firms will hire fewer juniors who can do it with a tool. But I'm better placed than most, because I already work this way, and I can sell that to a boss in about thirty seconds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn my freelancing into something that looks like a small business, with a name and a site, and offer finance automation to shops and clinics. I'd keep applying for jobs where I'd run the tools, not just use them. I'd save about half of what I earn, because I'd expect gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit wary, like standing at the top of a big slide. Fun, but you'd want to be sure of the landing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rather have the business or a regular job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you rather have the business or a regular job?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does sharing the gains look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both for a while. A job gives me a manager, colleagues and a reference, and the business gives me speed. If a graduate programme offered me a role with a real data focus I'd say yes, then keep two clients on the side.

say: I'd say AI takes the **drudge work** and leaves the judgment, and the gains should be shared.
I'd tell friends still applying to build something real.
think: Many entry jobs, including ones I'm applying for, will **shrink**.
I'm better placed because I already work this way.

Offer finance automation to shops and clinics.
Save about **half** of what I earn.

fieldNote: His **adaptability** shows: he treats disruption as a market.

Plans to hold a job and side clients together.

steps.text: Register a small business and build a simple website
Offer finance automation to shops and clinics
Save half of my freelance earnings each month
Take a graduate data role and keep two clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules and sharing of the gains, fast. Two years is nothing. I'd push for public ownership of some of the big models, or at least a tax that pays everyone a share. And I'd tell my friends to stop using it just for homework and start building things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my degree could be worth much less within two years, and I'm competing with the thing I use every day. The freelancing helps because I'm close to the tools, but a shop owner could also do it herself soon enough. My window is short and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on being useful. Sign up as many small clients as I can, build templates I can sell, and look for work at companies building these systems, in customer success or data roles. I'd also move money from savings into a small stock of equipment, like a better laptop and a second screen. And I'd ask my parents to keep the spare room for me for two more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of thrilling and sickening. I can see the opportunity, and I can also see the floor falling away under a lot of friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which friends are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if the shop owners can do it themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dani studied marketing, wrote copy for a small agency, and was let go last month when they brought in a tool. He's good, and it didn't matter. That's the kind of story I think hits everyone within a year or two.

say: I'd say we need **rules** and shared gains, such as a tax paying everyone a share.
I'd tell friends to stop using AI for homework and start building.
think: My degree may be worth much less within **two years**, and I'm competing with my daily tool.
Shop owners could soon do my freelance work themselves.

Look for customer success or data jobs at companies building these systems.

feel: **Thrilled** and sickened: I see the opportunity and the floor falling under friends.

fieldNote: Sees both sides: **opportunity** for himself, danger for peers.
Reasons from a real example, his friend Dani losing a copywriting job.
His cushion lets him bet on speed.

steps.text: Sign as many small clients as possible and sell templates
Apply for customer success and data roles at AI companies
Buy a better laptop and a second screen for freelance work
Keep living in the family spare room for two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the sweet spot for acting. I'd tell friends to pick a niche now, not in year four. And I'd tell the council and the college to start courses on working with AI, because there's a lot of people who'd show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the time. I could get a job in the next year, build a track record, and by 2031 either run a team that uses the tools or be running my own firm. I'd also keep one eye on the day the thinking jobs go, because after that the choices narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a graduate analyst role with a firm that has real data work, and I'd keep freelancing on weekends. I'd save for a deposit on a flat by about 26. I'd also join a local group of small business owners, so I have a network that doesn't depend on one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. A bit of pressure, which I like, and no panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean by the choices narrowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you mean by the choices narrowing?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join a group of small business owners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the software does nearly all thinking work, jobs mostly go to people who own things or manage people. So I want to own something by then, even if it's small, and be good with people. That's my plan for not ending up on the wrong side.

say: I'd say five years is the **sweet spot** for acting and tell friends to pick a niche now.
I'd ask the college to teach working with AI.
think: I'd use the time to build a track record, then run a **team** or my own firm by 2031.
After thinking jobs go, choices narrow.

S3.quote: I want to own something by then, even if it's small, and be good with people.

steps.text: Take a graduate analyst role at a firm with data work
Keep freelancing on weekends for local shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous and we should use it to redesign work, not just to wait. I'd tell people to push for shared ownership of what AI produces. And I'd tell friends to enjoy the next few years, because the next ten won't look like the last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel good. In ten years I'll be 33 with a decade of experience, and I'd probably be running something. The one thing that nags me is whether I'm really that special, or whether everyone with a laptop is on the same ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a role now, learn how a real firm works, and save aggressively for the first three years. Then I'd start a small consultancy with a friend, maybe with Dani, and hire people instead of replacing them. I'd keep volunteering with the food-truck co-op as a way to give back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light. I'm happy picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does hiring people instead of replacing them mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does hiring people instead of replacing them mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What nags you about everyone being on the same ramp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I run a small firm and the software can do the work of three juniors, I'd still keep two and train them, and use the extra time to serve more clients. It costs me a bit, but I'd sleep better, and I'd have people who know what I know.

say: I'd say ten years is generous, so we should **redesign work**, not just wait.
I'd urge shared ownership of what AI produces.
think: At 33 I'd have a decade of experience and **probably run** something.
I wonder whether I'm special or everyone with a laptop is on the same ramp.

Start a small consultancy with my friend Dani and keep the juniors I hire.

fieldNote: Optimism with an ethical edge: he wants to **hire** people, not just replace them.

steps.text: Take a graduate finance role and learn how a firm runs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, for sure. Two years doesn't give schools, firms or anyone a chance to catch up, and my friends who aren't tool people would be hit hardest. What would help is quick public training, shared ownership of what the machines make, and a decent safety net for those who lose jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as relaxed as I look. Being comfortable with technology gives me an edge, but the edge only lasts if the people around me are okay too.

headlineQuote: Being comfortable with technology gives me an edge, but the edge only lasts if the people around me are okay too.
portrait: Carlos is 23, a business and finance graduate in Port Selby with **40 applications** out and no offer.
He uses AI daily and earns **freelance income** building dashboards for small shops.
His progressive views show in his calls for shared gains and public training.
He treats disruption as a market, planning clients, templates and a small firm, but he worries about friends.
In the fast scenario he feels thrill and dread together; with ten years he turns light and **hopeful**.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries him most, because friends who aren't comfortable with tools would be hit hardest.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **public training**, shared ownership of what the machines produce and a safety net for people who lose jobs.
